text: The rwb-decision slice of RWB-E2-036 is the decision record of a placement and nothing else: this story consumes the placement fact on rwb.decision-record.v1, appends one D6 entry to decision_log_entry in its own transaction and serves the two decision-log reads. The caller-facing operation, the approved callers list, the feature flag, the request validation, the forwarding and the error mapping stay with RWB-P2-E2036-APP and RWB-P2-E2036-CON; the placement, the allocation method, the caseload cap, the overflow queue, the assignment and the local decision record of the placement transaction stay with rwb-case (P3); the right, the scope and the masking stay with rwb-access (P4). No legacy criterion is owned verbatim here (acs is empty) because every legacy AC of the key either performs the placement, checks the admission or asserts the allocation engine.
why: The legacy story puts the endpoint in the P2 backlog with the code in recovery/casewf/placement, which under 19 services is an admission concern of rwb-integration and a placement concern of rwb-case; the WP places this secondary slice in rwb-decision, so the only boundary that keeps one deliverable per story and satisfies the DP table is the record of the placement, and the record criteria must be new (D-RCV-60) because the admission and placement criteria are owned by the other slices.

text: The feature flag rwb.casewf.queue-placement gates the admission and never the ledger: a placement that committed always writes its central entry, and this story reads no flag of its own. Flag-off behaviour (404 with MSG-P2-025 and nothing changed) belongs to RWB-P2-E2036-APP.
why: The legacy flag exists so that no caller can place a case until a consumer is approved; once a placement has committed, suppressing its record would break BR5 and BR6 of the key and principle 5, so a flag on the record path would be a business-value change and not a realignment.

text: The decision code D6, the final-call form 'PLACED <queueCode>' and the element names of the placement fact and of the two ledger reads are reference data or contract elements read with the version in force, never constants in code; where no source names an element, the story carries the placeholder and names the fact by its role (case, decision code, model or agent version, inputs reference, reason, caller identity, queue and queue code, decided time, placement key) rather than inventing a field name.
why: DP-07 and BR-P7-001 forbid a business value in code and LOV-DECISION is named but never enumerated in FSD P7 v3 or TSD P7 v2; the fact is published by another service, so inventing element names here would create a second, incompatible contract.

text: One central entry per placement, enforced twice: the placement key carried on the fact is stored as the idempotency key of the entry and a unique key on it makes a second entry impossible, and the inbox mark of the delivery makes a repeat acknowledge and write nothing. A repeated caller request is refused 409 by the case side and never reaches this service.
why: Legacy AC7 and BR6 demand one entry however often the placement is delivered, and one transaction can no longer span the placement and the ledger, so the guarantee has to be a key on this side as well as the owner's unique placement key; without it a redelivery would consume a chain sequence.
